title: “But sir, is a river alive?”
author: Murray Sutcliffe
summary: Murray Sutcliffe uses Robert Macfarlane's question "Is a river alive?" to probe what tightly scripted teaching might cost. Drawing on Heidegger's remark that a hydroelectric plant changed how the Rhine appears, he argues that once a thing is valued only for its utility, our knowledge of it narrows to utility as well. Writing from beside the Mekong, he applies this to the current debate over Direct Instruction: he accepts that knowledge deserves to be prioritised and says he has changed his mind about the limits of inquiry learning, yet he worries about the questions that do not meet the brief of a scripted lesson. A method built to ensure students learn what we have decided matters, he suggests, is not a model for deciding what is worth knowing in the first place. He admits his own failure, when teaching Theory of Knowledge, to give weight to knowledge systems he judged inferior, and closes by hoping every pupil meets a teacher willing to put the script down.
points: Efficiency is only one measure of educational value, and a method designed to deliver predetermined content cannot also decide which questions are worth asking.
Scripted lessons carry an opportunity cost: each time a child is told to save a question for later, they move closer to not asking at all.
The author supports a knowledge-rich curriculum and Direct Instruction where its effectiveness is demonstrated, while cautioning against extending it beyond those purposes.
Heidegger's Rhine and Macfarlane's shifting baseline syndrome show how normalised framings narrow what we notice, a warning for teachers about their own inherited assumptions.
quotes: A scripted lesson decides in advance what students will learn and which questions it will pursue, but a good education gives pupils time to follow questions of their own.
The question that follows is what kind of education not only gives someone the knowledge to build something, but also the nerve to ask whether it should be built to begin with?
He is swimming against the current, asking what a river is, when the rest of the world is asking what a river is for.
However, I cannot shake this nagging sense that there must be an opportunity cost, the further we move towards tightly scripted lessons. And this is where Macfarlane comes in.

I worry about what happens when a student puts up their hand to ask a question that doesn’t meet the brief, and the teacher makes a snap judgment about where it might lead, concluding that they must stick to the script. Sometimes this might be entirely reasonable.

A method designed to ensure students learn what we have decided they need to know, is not necessarily a model for deciding what is worth knowing in the first place. Surely somewhere in education, there must be room for questions whose answers we haven’t already decided upon?
Curiosity might not be a prerequisite for learning, but it can fundamentally change what we want to learn in the first place. There’s value in following the stream far enough to see where it goes.

Even whilst teaching Theory of Knowledge in the IB, I gave less time to the optional theme of Knowledge & Indigenous Societies, because I couldn’t see its immediate value; it seemed to ask questions so far removed from the knowledge systems I was familiar with that I judged it inferior. I was teaching students to question the limits of knowledge, whilst failing to recognise the limits of my own.
